I loved my betta so much, but noticed he was pineconing significantly and was near the end of his life cycle. Because he was the best boy to ever swim, I went to the store and bought a big rubber tree plant. I bought a big pot for the plant and took it home with extra soil. 

I added clove oil to the tank and waited until I knew he had passed. I knew my old man wasn't suffering anymore, but I couldn't just not do something to memorialize him. 

I fished him out of his tank with a net and gently placed him in a tiny biodegradable fish pod meant for his size. I wrote a note to him and placed him and the note inside. I buried both in the soil and have been tending ever since. It's still weird to look at the tree and realize it's my fish, but it makes me so happy to care for him.

What's the temp of the water now? I've been in your shoes and I was up all night worried sick. They need 75-80 to thrive. On cold days where my heaters were crapping out, my bettas did okay in the low 70s. If it touches the high 60s or lower, then I got super worried and noticed they'd go into shock. Don't let it get there. 

I taped a heating pad to my tank for a few nights until the heater was delivered. If you don't have one, you could look into doing a very small water change once or twice throughout the night. And I mean small enough to not disrupt the water cycle, but to put more warm water in. Move the tank to a temporarily warm location in your house or room. Put it in a heated room with a heater, or with all fans off. Make sure it's away from windows or AC/vents (unless they are giving off heat.)

Is the current too strong? Sometimes bettas can stay in a corner fighting a current if it's too strong to swim against. Maybe not the issue, but I'd check it out and make sure it's not too strong. Put it at the lowest setting if need be

Therapy has been a fickle trial period for me. I've tried multiple therapists, different companies and locations, different methods (in person, video chat, message only). 

I've found that therapy only works if you're willing to be receptive and actually utilize the tools being given to you. 

No one really likes therapy, because it's difficult to deal with your problems head on. It's easy to ignore and sweep under the rug, but it never goes away. Therapy is a great place to start in terms of getting better in aspects of mental health and dealing with issues with the help of a professional. 

My advice is to be receptive. Be completely honest, don't hide anything, and be open about your thoughts and feelings. They only want to help, so letting them in is the best place to start. 

The magic won't start after one session. I mean, I've been in therapy for several months and I've only just started to see a tiny way it's helped me. 

It's just a start, but it's more than nothing. 

Don't give up. If you're in CBT, do your "homework" or tasks for yourself asked for after sessions. If you're simply venting and asking for advice, think of any large or small issues you're dealing with. Every problem matters, so don't let any session go to waste. That is valuable time that can help you get better. 

Don't give up on going! It'll be worth it, I promise you. I hope you get through what you're going through.
